segments.english: God said, "Let the earth bring forth living creatures, each according to its kind: livestock and crawling things and the wild animals of the earth, each according to its kind." And so it was.
segments.literal: and-said God let-bring-forth the-earth creature-of living to-its-kind livestock and-crawler and-animal-of-earth to-its-kind and-was so

tokens.note: plural form with singular sense; the verb is singular
Hifil jussive, 3rd feminine singular, with the earth as subject: a command in the third person
נֶפֶשׁ is a living being; it stands in apposition to חַיָּה
the suffix is feminine singular and looks back to נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה
BDB lists only sense 3, wild beasts, which does not fit; Ibn Ezra takes בְּהֵמָה as the animals that live with people, so no listed sense is given
Rashi: low creatures that move along the ground; the pack's entry lists no senses
construct, with an old ending ־וֹ that is not a separate word

phrases.literal: 'creature-of living': a living being, used of the whole class

phrases.english: and the wild animals of the earth
phrases.literal: 'and-animal-of earth'; the ־וֹ on the construct is an old ending

grammar: תּוֹצֵא is a Hifil jussive: the earth is addressed in the third person, 'let the earth cause to come out'.
The list has three kinds, בְּהֵמָה, רֶמֶשׂ and חַיְתוֹ־אֶרֶץ, joined by ו except for the first.
חַיְתוֹ is the construct of חַיָּה with an extra final ו; Ibn Ezra and Radak compare בְּנוֹ בְעֹר (Num 24:3).
The etnaḥta on the second לְמִינָהּ divides the command from וַיְהִי־כֵן.
The suffix of לְמִינָהּ is feminine singular, agreeing with נֶפֶשׁ: one 'living being' brought out kind by kind.
segments.note: Rashi says the earth needed only to bring out what was created on the first day, so the English says 'bring forth', not 'create'. The three kinds follow Ibn Ezra and Rashi: livestock live with people; crawling things are small and low; wild animals live where no one settles. 'Each according to its kind' is repeated because the Hebrew repeats it.

commentary.summary: Rashi: as I explained, everything was created on the first day, and the earth only needed to bring them out. The English 'bring forth' renders the Hifil without 'create'.
Rashi: נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה means that it has life. The English 'living creatures' keeps this.
Rashi: רֶמֶשׂ are swarmers, low creatures that creep on the earth and seem dragged along, since their going is not noticeable. The English 'crawling things' adopts this.
Ibn Ezra: the clause is a general term for what fire, water and earth bring forth, the human included. It bears on the structure of the chapter, not on the English wording.
Ibn Ezra: בְּהֵמָה are those that are with people, for riding and eating. The English 'livestock' follows.
Ibn Ezra: רֶמֶשׂ are the small ones that go on the earth.
Ibn Ezra: wild animals are those in the open country where no one settles, and the last ו of וחיתו is an added letter, as in בנו בעור. The English 'wild animals of the earth' follows.
Ramban: בְּהֵמָה are the grazing kinds, tame or wild. The English keeps Ibn Ezra's 'livestock'; Ramban's wider sense is recorded.

apparatus: Ramban reads בְּהֵמָה as all grazers and חַיָּה as meat-eaters, tame or wild; the English takes Ibn Ezra's sense.

segments.english: God made the wild animals of the earth, each according to its kind, and the livestock according to its kind, and every crawling thing of the ground according to its kind. And God saw that it was good.
segments.literal: and-made God [object-mark] animal-of the-earth to-its-kind and-[object-mark] the-livestock to-its-kind and-[object-mark] all-of crawler-of the-ground to-its-kind and-saw God that-good

tokens.note: BDB lists only sense 3, wild beasts, which does not fit; see 1:24.8
construct; the pack's entry lists no senses
the suffix is masculine here (־הוּ), agreeing with the masculine רֶמֶשׂ

phrases.english: the wild animals of the earth
and every crawling thing of the ground

grammar: Each of the three objects is introduced by אֵת and followed by לְמִינָהּ (לְמִינֵהוּ for the masculine רֶמֶשׂ).
Verse 24 asked the earth to 'bring forth'; this verse says וַיַּעַשׂ, 'and God made'. Radak explains why the making follows וַיְהִי־כֵן.
רֶמֶשׂ הָאֲדָמָה uses 'ground' where verse 24 used 'earth'.
כִּי־טוֹב has no verb; the English adds 'it was'.
The etnaḥta on לְמִינֵהוּ divides the making from the verdict.
segments.note: Rashi takes וַיַּעַשׂ as 'he set them right in their beauty and stature'; the English keeps the plain 'made', which allows that sense.

commentary.summary: Rashi: וַיַּעַשׂ means he fixed them in their beauty and in their stature. The English keeps 'made' and takes it as God fitting each kind, not only producing it.

segments.english: God said, "Let us make humankind in our image, after our likeness, and let them rule over the fish of the sea and the birds of the sky and the livestock and all the earth and every crawling thing that crawls on the earth."
segments.literal: and-said God let-us-make human in-our-image like-our-likeness and-let-them-rule in-fish-of the-sea and-in-bird-of the-sky and-in-the-livestock and-in-all-of the-earth and-in-all-of the-crawler the-crawling on the-earth

tokens.note: 1st person plural; see the note on the plural
no article: 'a human', here a class; the plural 'them' follows
in-image-of-us. Rashi: בִּדְפוּס שֶׁלָּנוּ, 'in our mold'.
jussive plural; Rashi hears here both רדה 'rule' and ירד 'go down'
BDB sense 3, wild beasts, does not fit here
Radak: 'all the earth' means the beasts of the earth, the wild animals that live outside settled land; Ramban: rule over the earth itself, to uproot, dig and quarry.
participle used as an attribute: 'the one that crawls'

phrases.literal: 'like-likeness-of-us'; the כ is the kaf of resemblance

phrases.english: and the birds of the sky

grammar: נַעֲשֶׂה is 1st person plural: Rashi and Ibn Ezra both take it as God speaking with the angels (Rashi: his court); the royal plural, which Ibn Ezra reports from the Gaon, he rejects. The English keeps 'us'.
אָדָם has no article, so 'a human' or 'humankind', not yet a name; the article comes in 1:27.
בְּצַלְמֵנוּ and כִּדְמוּתֵנוּ stand side by side with no ו: 'in our image, like our likeness'.
וְיִרְדּוּ is a plural jussive, so the one אָדָם is collective. The root רדה sounds like ירד, 'go down' (Rashi).
Five domains of rule are listed: fish, birds, livestock, all the earth, and crawling things.
segments.note: The plural 'Let us make': Rashi takes it as God taking counsel with his heavenly court, to teach humility; Ibn Ezra rejects the Niphal reading and the Gaon's royal plural, and reads God speaking to the angels. The English keeps 'us'. 'Humankind' is used because אָדָם has no article and the following verb is plural; 1:27 then has הָאָדָם. 'All the earth' follows the Hebrew word for word; Radak reads it as the wild animals of the earth.

commentary.summary: Rashi: we learn God's humility here. Since the human is in the likeness of the angels and they would be jealous, God consulted them; a king deciding a case consults his court, as in Micaiah's vision before Ahab. The English keeps 'us' as a true plural.

Rashi: although they did not help in forming the human, Scripture teaches courtesy and humility, that the great consults and takes leave of the small. Had it said 'I will make', we would not learn this; the answer to the heretics is written beside it: 'and God created' (singular).
Rashi: בְּצַלְמֵנוּ means in our mold (בדפוס שלנו). The English 'image' renders צֶלֶם and this sense goes in the notes.
Rashi: כִּדְמוּתֵנוּ means to understand and to discern. The English 'likeness' keeps דְּמוּת.

Rashi: the word carries both rule and descent: if he is worthy, he rules over the animals; if not, he goes down before them and the animal rules over him. The English takes 'rule', as the context requires, and the second sense is kept here.

Ibn Ezra: some take נעשה as a Niphal participle (Neh 5:18) and 'in our image' as Moses' words; he calls this lacking sense. He reports the Gaon (image = rule; the plural is how kings speak, citing Gen 29:27, Dan 2:36, Num 22:6) and rejects those proof texts as 'false witnesses'. His own reading: God said to the angels, 'Let us make a human; we will busy ourselves with him, not the water and the earth'; the image is the human's upper soul, which does not die, and בְּצֶלֶם אֱלֹהִים means the image of an angel.
Ramban: because the human is male and female, he says 'let them rule'.
Radak: 'all the earth' means the animals of the earth, the wild animals not in settled land, as it is called חַיַּת הָאָרֶץ.

apparatus: Plural 'us': Rashi (God and his court) and Ibn Ezra (God and the angels) agree; the royal plural of the Gaon, reported and rejected by Ibn Ezra, is not adopted.
Radak reads 'all the earth' as 'the wild animals of the earth'; this is not adopted in the English.

segments.english: God created the human in his image; in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them.
segments.literal: and-created God [object-mark] the-human in-his-image in-image-of God created him male and-female created them

with the article: the human of 1:26
qatal after the wayyiqtol: the same act restated

object marker with a masculine plural suffix

phrases.english: in the image of God he created him

grammar: The verse has three lines: God created the human in his image; in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them.
הָאָדָם now has the article: it points back to the indefinite אָדָם of 1:26. It is not yet a proper name.
The object suffix changes from singular (אֹתוֹ) to plural (אֹתָם): one human, then male and female.
The first בָּרָא is a wayyiqtol; the next two are qatal and restate the act.
בְּצַלְמוֹ and בְּצֶלֶם אֱלֹהִים use the same noun: 'his image' and 'the image of God'.
segments.note: The suffix of 'in his image' could refer to God or to the human; Rashi takes the image as a mold made for the human, and says that mold is the likeness of his maker. The English keeps 'his', as the Hebrew does. 'Male and female' is read as the plain sense that both were created on the sixth day.

commentary.summary: Rashi: 'in a mold made for him'; everything was created by word, but the human by hands (Ps 139:5); he was made with a seal, like a coin struck with a die. The English keeps 'in his image'; the mold sense goes in the notes.
Rashi: Scripture explains that the image prepared for him is the image of the likeness of his maker. The English 'in the image of God' follows.

Rashi: the plain meaning is that here we are told both were created on the sixth day, with how explained elsewhere; the midrash says he was made with two faces and then divided. The English 'male and female' follows the plain meaning.

apparatus: The suffix of בְּצַלְמוֹ ('in his image') is not fixed by the Hebrew: God or the human. The next clause names God.

segments.english: God blessed them, and God said to them, "Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth and subdue it, and rule over the fish of the sea and the birds of the sky and every living thing that crawls on the earth."
segments.literal: and-blessed [object-mark]-them God and-said to-them God be-fruitful and-multiply and-fill [object-mark] the-earth and-subdue-it and-rule in-fish-of the-sea and-in-bird-of the-sky and-in-all-of living the-crawling on the-earth

the subject is named a second time
Qal imperative plural; the pack's BDB extract lists only Hiphil senses, so no sense is given.
imperative with a feminine singular suffix; written without the ו of the verb (Rashi)
feminine participle with the article, agreeing with חַיָּה

phrases.english: and rule over the fish of the sea
and the birds of the sky
and every living thing that crawls on the earth

grammar: The blessing is stated first (וַיְבָרֶךְ אֹתָם), then the speech (וַיֹּאמֶר לָהֶם); the zinor and segol close the blessing sentence.
The imperatives are all plural: פְּרוּ, רְבוּ, מִלְאוּ, כִבְשֻׁהָ, רְדוּ.
וְכִבְשֻׁהָ is written without the second ו of the verb form; Rashi draws a lesson from the spelling.
After the etnaḥta on וְכִבְשֻׁהָ, the second half opens with וּרְדוּ: rule over three domains, fish, birds and every living thing that crawls, where 1:26 listed five.
חַיָּה הָרֹמֶשֶׂת has a feminine participle, where 1:26 had masculine הָרֹמֵשׂ.
segments.note: The pack parses פְּרוּ as Qal, while its BDB extract lists only Hiphil senses, so no sense is given; the translation is 'be fruitful' either way. Rashi's reading of the defective וְכִבְשֻׁהָ is a homily on the spelling.

commentary.summary: Rashi: וכבשה lacks a ו to teach that the male subdues the female so that she will not be a gadabout, and that the man, who is used to subduing, is commanded to be fruitful and multiply, not the woman. This is drawn from the spelling and does not change the English 'subdue it'.

segments.english: God said, "See, I have given you every plant bearing seed that is on the surface of the whole earth, and every tree that has in it fruit of a tree bearing seed. It shall be yours for food."
segments.literal: and-said God see I-have-given to-you [object-mark] all-of herb sowing seed which on face-of all-of the-earth and-[object-mark] all-of the-tree which-in-it fruit-of tree sowing seed to-you it-shall-be for-food

tokens.note: הִנֵּה, a particle that draws attention; the English 'see' does the job without filler
עֵשֶׂב, herbage; the pack's entry lists no senses
'face of'; פָּנִים is plural in form
yiqtol, 3rd masculine singular; the subject is the whole gift
לְ + אָכְלָה, 'to eating'; BDB lists only 'devouring' and 'consuming', which do not suit, so no listed sense is given

phrases.english: that is on the surface of the whole earth

phrases.literal: 'which in-it fruit-of'; the relative clause is in the Hebrew order

grammar: הִנֵּה with the qatal נָתַתִּי presents a gift already made: 'See, I have given'. Radak: as if 'I hereby give', or 'when I created them, I gave them to you'.
עֵשֶׂב זֹרֵעַ זֶרַע and פְּרִי־עֵץ זֹרֵעַ זָרַע are parallel, each a participle with its cognate noun: 'seed-sowing seed'.
The zaqef qaton on הָאָרֶץ divides the plants from the trees; the revia on זֶרַע sets off the relative clause אֲשֶׁר עַל־פְּנֵי כָל־הָאָרֶץ; the etnaḥta on זָרַע ends the gift.
יִהְיֶה is singular: 'it shall be', with the whole gift as one subject, not each plant.
לְאָכְלָה is 'for food'; the commentators note that this verse does not yet allow meat.
segments.note: The verb זֹרֵעַ is 'sowing' and the English 'bears seed' renders the sense; the cognate noun is in English 'seed'. The commentators agree that the gift is plants only; the English says nothing about meat, which is not in the Hebrew.

commentary.summary: Rashi: he put cattle and wild animals on a par with them in food, and did not allow the human and his wife to kill a creature and eat flesh; all of them together were to eat only green herbs. When the sons of Noah came, he permitted flesh to them (Gen 9:3). The English 'for food', with plants alone, follows this.

Ibn Ezra: he permitted people, and everything with a living soul, to eat every herb; every tree fruit is permitted to people; the green herb is for the animals and for everything that crawls; meat was not permitted until after the flood. The English follows: the human has the plants and the fruit.

segments.english: And to every wild animal of the earth and to every bird of the sky and to everything that crawls on the earth, in which there is a living soul, I have given every green plant for food. And so it was.
segments.literal: and-to-all-of animal-of the-earth and-to-all-of bird-of the-sky and-to-all-of crawling on the-earth which-in-it soul living [object-mark] all-of green herb to-food and-was so

tokens.note: construct, with the prefix לְ: 'to all of'
נֶפֶשׁ, the breathing life; with חַיָּה, 'a living soul'
marks the object of a verb not repeated from 1:29
יֶרֶק, greenness; no senses in the pack

phrases.english: And to every wild animal of the earth
and to every bird of the sky
and to everything that crawls on the earth
in which there is a living soul
phrases.literal: 'which-in-it soul living': the breath of life within it
object marker: the verb 'I have given' is carried over from 1:29, since the Hebrew has none here

grammar: The verse has no verb of giving; it takes נָתַתִּי from 1:29 and אֶת marks its object.
The three groups are the same as in 1:26 and 1:28: wild animals, birds, crawling things; here without fish.
אֲשֶׁר־בּוֹ נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה, 'in which is a living soul', describes the animals as having the breath of life, which the plants they eat do not have (Radak).
The telisha gedola on הָאָרֶץ is a rare doubled accent mark.
The English adds 'I have given' where the Hebrew has an object marker and no verb.
segments.note: The Hebrew leaves out the verb 'I have given', so the English supplies it from 1:29 in the phrase that holds the object marker. The relative clause 'in which there is a living soul' stands after 'everything that crawls on the earth' and the English keeps it there; it can be read of all three groups.
apparatus: The relative clause 'in which is a living soul' could limit only the crawling things or the three groups together; the English keeps the Hebrew order.

segments.english: God saw everything that he had made, and indeed it was very good. And there was evening and there was morning, the sixth day.
segments.literal: and-saw God [object-mark] all-of which he-made and-behold-good very and-was evening and-was morning day-of the-sixth

tokens.note: qatal, a completed act before the seeing; 'he had made'
וְהִנֵּה, 'and behold', marks what God found

the pack parses יוֹם as construct; Ibn Ezra rejects the construct reading ('day of the sixth sphere') and takes it as a noun with an ordinal that has the article: 'a day, the sixth', as אִישׁ הַיִּשְׂרְאֵלִי (Lev 24:10)
article on the ordinal after an indefinite noun: 'the sixth day'

grammar: The refrain of the days is 'and there was evening and there was morning', here with 'the sixth day', which is the only day in this chapter with the article.
וְהִנֵּה־טוֹב מְאֹד adds 'very' and וְהִנֵּה to the refrain 'and God saw that it was good' of the earlier days.
The qatal עָשָׂה ('he had made') looks back over the whole of the six days.

In יוֹם הַשִּׁשִּׁי the ordinal has the article and יוֹם does not. The pack parses יוֹם as construct; Ibn Ezra reads 'the day that is sixth', a noun followed by an articled adjective, as in אִישׁ הַיִּשְׂרְאֵלִי (Lev 24:10).
The paragraph mark פ closes the account of the sixth day.
segments.note: The article on 'the sixth' day is the Hebrew's, and the English follows it with 'the sixth day'. Rashi's homily on the added ה (the sixth day of Sivan, the giving of the Torah) does not bear on the plain sense.

commentary.summary: Rashi: the added ה on יוֹם הַשִּׁשִּׁי means God made a condition with creation that Israel would accept the five books of the Torah; or: everything hangs until the sixth of Sivan. This is homily and does not bear on the English.

Ibn Ezra: some say יוֹם in יוֹם הַשִּׁשִּׁי is in the construct state (סמוך) and the sense is 'the day of the sixth sphere'; this is not true. It means the day that is sixth from the first day, so also יוֹם הַשְּׁבִיעִי: a noun followed by an adjective with the article, as אִישׁ הַיִּשְׂרְאֵלִי (Lev 24:10), and רְקִיעַ הַשָּׁמַיִם (1:20), 'the firmament that is heaven'. The English 'the sixth day' follows this.

apparatus: The paragraph mark פ follows this verse.
